transcript.question: What happens when you add a new drone to the fleet or retire an old one?
transcript.answer: I add new drones to the fleet and retire old ones, while keeping the drones and charging equipment in working order. transcript.question: Walk me through an ordinary working day for you, from the moment you start until you finish.
transcript.answer: I plan and run our flights, and as a licensed dispatcher, I am responsible for each flight by deciding which drone flies along which way and signing off before it leaves. Several of us plan at the same time for the same busy sites and popular drones, and I can call off a flight. Before and outside my control, things happen like loads being ready or not, and drones reaching their points and arriving.

transcript.answer: I worry about sudden airspace closures and planned ones coming into force while drones from several companies are already in the air, and these closures are often amended during the day. Radio coverage is patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, and battery drains faster in cold and wind than planned. Links used to give instructions to drones and charging equipment are unreliable, so an instruction can get through twice when the sender cannot tell if the first attempt arrived.

transcript.question: Walk me through an ordinary working day at the airspace desk, from the moment you start until you finish.
transcript.answer: I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which includes the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones grouping them, and the closures announced by the authorities. The authorities define zones where flying is prohibited, and they announce planned closures with a start and end time, as well as sudden ones that apply at once. These closures are often amended during the day, such as when an area is widened or an end time moves, and a closure can even come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.

transcript.question: What happens to the shared picture when an authority amends a closure during the day?

transcript.question: Is there anything about how flight corridors, sites, or prohibited zones interact with the companies' flights that you haven't mentioned yet?
transcript.answer: Drones fly along corridors between named sites. Sites have only so many places where drones can take off and land at the same time. Drones fly on their own autopilots, and people on the ground supervise them without steering them with a stick through this service.

transcript.answer: A closure can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air. The authorities define zones where flying is prohibited, and they announce closures with a start and end time or sudden ones that apply at once. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.

transcript.answer: I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which consists of the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. Beyond this, I do not do anything else with the shared picture that we have not talked about.

items.requirement: The service must keep each company's fleet, charging pads, site operations, jobs, flights, and operational problems isolated so that no company can view or use another company's operational data.
The service must prevent the airspace desk from viewing any individual company's fleet, jobs, sites, flights, or operational problems.

The service must maintain a single shared airspace picture visible across all companies, containing named sites, the network of flight corridors between them, the zones grouping those corridors, authority-defined prohibited zones, and airspace closures.
The service must allow a fleet technician to add new drones to a company's fleet and retire old drones from it across multiple models and manufacturers.
The service must record for each drone model its carrying capacity, flight range on a full battery, carried sensors, and charging connector type.
The service must allow a fleet technician to take a drone out of service for repairs and put it back into service once repairs are complete.
The service must prevent retired drones and drones taken out of service for repairs from being assigned to a flight or signed off for departure.
The service must record all repairs and servicing performed on a company's drones and charging equipment so the company can show regulators how its drones have been looked after.

The service must allow a fleet technician to set up and manage a company's charging pads at the company's own sites, recording each pad's supported charging connector type and whether it is in working order.
The service must prevent a company's charging pads from being lent to, assigned to, or used by drones from any other company.

The service must allow a drone to be sent to charge only at a charging pad that belongs to the same company, is in working order, and uses the same non-interchangeable charging connector type as the drone.

The service must allow a dispatcher to plan a flight by assigning an available drone to a route along flight corridors between named sites, checking that the drone's carrying capacity, carried sensors, and battery range match the planned flight.
The service must account for faster battery drain in cold and wind when checking whether a drone has sufficient range for a planned flight and when monitoring a flight in progress.
The service must require a licensed dispatcher to sign off on a flight before the drone is permitted to depart.
The service must allow a dispatcher to call off a planned or active flight.
The service must allow multiple dispatchers within the same company to plan flights concurrently while preventing conflicting assignments of the same drone.
The service must track the maximum number of drones that can take off and land at the same time at each site and prevent concurrent flight plans from exceeding that site capacity.
The service must support ground supervision of drones flying on their own autopilots and must not provide manual stick-steering controls for flying drones.
The service must accept and display status reports from external people and devices during a flight, including whether the load is ready, when the drone reaches its points, and when it arrives.
The service must prevent flights from being planned through authority-defined prohibited zones or active airspace closures.
The service must allow the airspace desk to enter planned airspace closures with a start time and an end time, as well as sudden closures that take effect immediately.
